entry: Ester of [[Fatty acid|fatty acids]], or a mixture of such compounds, most commonly those that occur in living beings or in food. The term often refers specifically to triglycerides, the main components of vegetable oils and of animal fatty tissue. Fats are one of the three main macronutrient groups in the human diet, along with [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]] and proteins, and are the main components of common foods such as milk, butter, lard and cooking oils. Each gram of fat releases about nine food calories (37 kJ = 8.8 kcal) when burned or metabolized. Fats store energy, insulate body organs and help maintain body temperature. Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and can be absorbed only together with fats. Apart from a few essential fatty acids, the body can produce the fat it requires from other food ingredients.

Complex form of mirage visible in a narrow band just above the horizon, often seen in the Italian Strait of Messina. The name is the Italian translation of Morgan le Fay, the Arthurian enchantress by whose magic the mirages were described as fairy castles. A Fata Morgana distorts distant objects such as boats, islands and coastlines, often beyond recognition, and stacks inverted and upright images that change rapidly. It requires an atmospheric duct, formed when a layer of warmer air lies over colder dense air and acts as a refracting lens.

Male parent of a child, whether biological, adoptive or step. A biological father is the male genetic contributor, through sexual intercourse or [[Sperm|sperm]] donation, and may have legal obligations such as monetary support even when he does not raise the child. A stepfather is married to a child's parent but generally lacks the legal rights and responsibilities of a parent, while an [[Adoption|adoptive]] father becomes the parent through the legal process of adoption. Paid paternity leave first began in Sweden in 1976 and is paid in more than half of [[European Union]] countries. In almost all cultures fathers have been regarded as secondary caregivers, a perception that is slowly changing. Fathers' rights movements, such as Fathers 4 Justice, argue that family courts are biased against fathers.

Initiation and propagation of cracks in a material due to repeated loading. Once a fatigue crack forms, it grows a small amount with each cycle, typically leaving striations on the fracture surface, until it reaches a critical size and the structure fractures rapidly. Fatigue damage occurs at stresses far below a material's yield strength, usually starting at [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]] concentrations such as holes, persistent slip bands or grain boundaries in metals. The term metal fatigue reflects its traditional association with metal parts, and a 19th-century belief that railway axles failed because the metal had crystallized has since been disproved. Most materials, including composites, [[Plastic|plastics]] and [[Ceramic|ceramics]], also fail through fatigue. To predict fatigue life, engineers test coupons under constant-amplitude cyclic loading and average the crack growth over thousands of cycles.

Daughter of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]] and his wife Khadija, revered as a central figure in Islam. Her husband was [[Ali]], who is regarded as the first Shia imam, and her sons Hasan and Husayn were the second and third Shia imams. Her most common epithet, al-Zahra ("the radiant"), is central to Shia belief, and in both Shia and Sunni collections of hadith she is called Sayyidat Nisa' al-Janna ("mistress of the women of paradise"). Muhammad is said to have regarded her as the best of women and the dearest person to him. She is often viewed as an archetype for Muslim women, an example of compassion, generosity and endurance of suffering, and has been compared to [[Mary, mother of Jesus]], especially in [[Shia Islam]]. Through Fatima, Muhammad's family line has survived to the present, and her name remains a popular choice for Muslim girls.

Isma'ili Shi'a caliphate that ruled North Africa, Egypt and parts of West Asia from 909 to 1171. Its rulers claimed descent from the prophet Muhammad through his daughter [[Fatima]] and her husband [[Ali]]. The state was founded after Abu Abdallah led Kutama tribal forces against the Aghlabids in Ifriqiya, and Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah became the first caliph in 909. The capital moved to al-Mahdiyya in 921 and to al-Mansuriyya in 948. After conquering Egypt in 969, the Fatimids made [[Cairo]] their capital in 973. At its height the caliphate included Egypt, parts of the Maghreb, [[Sicily]], the Levant and the Hejaz, and it allowed a degree of religious tolerance towards non-Shi'a Muslims, Jews and Christians. After a civil war in the 1060s and encroachment by Seljuk Turks and Crusaders, the caliphate declined rapidly. In 1171 [[Saladin]] abolished the dynasty and founded the Ayyubid dynasty.

[[Carboxylic acid]] with an aliphatic chain, either saturated or unsaturated. Most naturally occurring fatty acids have an unbranched chain of an even number of carbon atoms, from 4 to 28. They make up up to 70% by weight of the [[Lipid|lipids]] in some microalgae, and in most organisms occur as esters in triglycerides, phospholipids and cholesteryl esters. Short-chain fatty acids have tails of five or fewer carbons, while very long-chain ones have 22 or more. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, and stearic acid, when neutralized with sodium hydroxide, is the most common form of [[Soap|soap]]. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds; cis bonds bend the chain and increase membrane fluidity, whereas trans fats are mostly the product of human processing such as hydrogenation, though some occur naturally in the milk and meat of ruminants. The concept was introduced by Michel Eugène Chevreul in 1813.

Planar fracture or discontinuity in a volume of rock across which significant displacement has occurred. Large faults in Earth's [[Crust (geology)|crust]] result from plate tectonic forces, with the largest forming the boundaries between [[Plate tectonics|plates]], such as the megathrust faults of subduction zones and transform faults. Rapid movement on active faults releases the energy that causes most [[Earthquake|earthquakes]], although some faults slip slowly by aseismic creep. Friction locks a fault until stress builds beyond its strength, and the fault then ruptures, releasing strain energy partly as seismic waves. On a non-vertical fault, the hanging wall lies above the fault plane and the footwall below; in reverse faults the hanging wall moves up, and in normal faults it moves down. A fault zone is a cluster of parallel faults or the zone of crushed rock along a single fault.

Protagonist of a classic German legend based on Johann Georg Faust, a magician and alchemist. The learned Faust, dissatisfied with the limits of science, theology and the humanities, makes a bargain with the [[Devil]] at a crossroads, exchanging his soul for knowledge and worldly pleasures. The devil's representative, Mephistopheles, serves him for 24 years, after which the early versions have Faust damned and carried off to Hell. The story was popularized in England by [[Christopher Marlowe]], whose *The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus* (c. 1592) gave it a classic treatment. In [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe|Goethe]]'s reworking, Faust is saved through his constant striving and the virtue of pure-hearted women. "Faust" and the adjective "Faustian" imply sacrificing spiritual values for power, knowledge or material gain.

British television [[Sitcom|sitcom]] by [[John Cleese]] and Connie Booth, broadcast on [[BBC]] Two in 1975 and 1979. Set in a dysfunctional hotel in Torquay, [[Devon]], it was inspired by the owner of a hotel where the [[Monty Python]] group stayed in 1970. Its farcical plots center on the tense owner Basil Fawlty and his bossy wife Sybil. The British Film Institute ranked it first among the 100 Greatest British Television Programmes in 2000, and a 2019 Radio Times panel of comedy experts named it the greatest British TV sitcom.

Method of transmitting scanned printed material, such as text or images, over a telephone line (short for facsimile). The document is scanned into a bitmap, sent as audio tones, and printed by the receiving machine. From the 1980s most machines compressed the data so that all-white or all-black areas were sent more quickly. Fax machines became ubiquitous in offices in the 1980s and 1990s, but have largely been replaced by [[Email|email]] and the [[World Wide Web|web]], though they remain in some medical administration and law enforcement settings.

American actress, winner of an Academy Award for *Network* (1976). Her breakthrough came as the outlaw Bonnie Parker beside [[Warren Beatty]] in *Bonnie and Clyde* (1967), which earned her first Academy Award nomination. Other films include *Chinatown* (1974), for which she received a second nomination, and *Mommie Dearest* (1981), in which she portrayed [[Joan Crawford]]. She has also won a Primetime Emmy Award, three Golden Globe Awards and a BAFTA Award.

Hong Kong singer-songwriter and actress. Her debut album, *Shirley Wong* (1989), was in Cantonese, and her breakthrough came with the Cantopop song "Fragile Woman" in 1992. Since the late 1990s she has recorded mainly in Mandarin. In 2000 [[Guinness World Records]] recognized her as the best-selling Cantopop female artist. She is best known in the West for her roles in [[Wong Kar-wai]]'s *Chungking Express* (1994) and *2046* (2004). After her second marriage in 2005 she withdrew from the limelight, making only occasional stage appearances.

Epidermal growth forming the outer covering, or plumage, of [[Bird|birds]] and some non-avian [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]]. Feathers are among the most complex integumentary structures in vertebrates. They aid flight, thermal insulation and waterproofing, while coloration helps with communication and protection. Vaned feathers cover the body, down feathers lie beneath them, and the remiges and rectrices of the wings and tail are the most important for flight. Feathers form in follicles in the epidermis and are made of tough β-keratin proteins. Goose and eider down have great loft, trapping insulating air, and quill pens were once made from large bird feathers. Hunting birds for ornamental feathers endangered some species, and feathers used in fashion today are a waste product of poultry farming.

Solid or semisolid remains of food that was not digested in the small intestine and was broken down by bacteria in the [[Large intestine|large intestine]]. Feces are discharged through the anus or cloaca during defecation. Their odor comes from skatole and sulfur-containing thiols, among other compounds. Although lower in energy than the original food, feces may retain about 50% of that energy, and many organisms feed on them, from bacteria to [[Dung beetle|dung beetles]]. Feces can be used as fertilizer, burned as fuel or dried for construction, and fecal transplants are used in medicine.

U.S. federal law enforcement agency and the domestic intelligence and security service of the United States, part of the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]]. It has jurisdiction over more than 200 categories of federal crimes and leads counterterrorism, counterintelligence and cybercrime investigations. Founded in 1908 as the Bureau of Investigation and renamed in 1935, it maintains 56 field offices and is headquartered in [[Washington, D.C.]] Its history includes the [[COINTELPRO]] program (1956–1971), which used covert actions against perceived domestic subversives and drew criticism.

Central banking system of the United States, created by the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, after a series of financial panics. Congress set three monetary objectives: maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates. The Federal Open Market Committee sets policy by adjusting the federal funds rate target, and twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks supervise privately owned commercial banks. Supporters credit its lender-of-last-resort actions with stabilizing the financial system in 2008, while critics point to more than 9,000 bank failures from 1930 to 1933 and to its approach to [[Inflation|inflation]].

headword: Federal government of the United States
sort_key: federal government of the united states
entry: National government of the United States, with legislative, executive and judicial branches defined by the [[Constitution of the United States|Constitution]], in effect since 1789. It shares sovereignty with each of the 50 states in a federal division of power. Its branches are Congress, the presidency and federal agencies, and the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] and subordinate federal courts. Indigenous tribes are recognized as having sovereign powers while remaining subject to federal jurisdiction. "Washington" and "White House" are sometimes used as metonyms for the government.

Mode of government that combines a central government with regional sub-unit governments, such as states, provinces or cantons, and divides powers between the two levels. Federalism differs from confederalism, in which the central government is subordinate to the regional states, and from the unitary state, in which the regions are subordinate to the central government even after a devolution of powers. Johannes Althusius and Montesquieu are considered the fathers of modern federalism. The first modern federal union was formed by states of the Old Swiss Confederacy in the mid-14th century. Federal systems today include Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, [[Germany]], India, Mexico, Nigeria, Russia, [[Switzerland]] and the [[United States]]. James Madison described the new U.S. Constitution as "neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both."

Conservative and nationalist American political party, the first known political party in the United States. It dominated the national government from 1789 to 1801 under the leadership of [[Alexander Hamilton]], whose policies included a national bank, tariffs and good relations with [[Great Britain]], expressed in the Jay Treaty of 1794. Its only president was [[John Adams]]. The party was defeated in 1800 by the [[Democratic-Republican Party]] and kept its stronghold in New England. It opposed the [[War of 1812]], briefly revived, and collapsed after its last presidential candidate in 1816.

Island country in [[Oceania]], consisting of four states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, that span the western Pacific just north of the [[Equator|equator]]. The states comprise around 607 islands with a combined land area of approximately 702 sq km (271 sq mi), but its waters occupy nearly 3 million sq km, giving it the 14th-largest exclusive economic zone in the world. The capital is Palikir, on Pohnpei Island. The islands were part of the former United Nations Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States from 1947 to 1994. The country became independent on November 3, 1986, under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and has a seat in the [[United Nations]].

Political union of partially self-governing provinces, states or other regions under a federal government. The self-governing status of the component units and the division of power between them and the central government are constitutionally entrenched and cannot be altered unilaterally. Federations are often multi-ethnic and cover large territories, such as [[Russia]], the [[United States]] and [[India]], but size is not required, as in Saint Kitts and Nevis and the [[Federated States of Micronesia]]. France and Japan are [[Unitary state|unitary states]]. Germany, with 16 states, and Nigeria, with 36 states and a federal capital territory, are federations. Roughly 40 per cent of the world's population lives in countries described as federal.

Italian film director and screenwriter known for a style that blends fantasy and baroque images with earthiness. Sight & Sound ranks his *8½* (1963) as the 10th-greatest film of all time. His best-known films include *I Vitelloni* (1953), *La Strada* (1954), *Nights of Cabiria* (1957), *La Dolce Vita* (1960), which won the Palme d'Or, and *Amarcord* (1973). He was nominated for 17 [[Academy Awards]], winning four, all in the Best Foreign Language Film category, a record. He also received an honorary statuette for lifetime achievement at the 65th Academy Awards. Later films include *Juliet of the Spirits* (1965), *Fellini Satyricon* (1969), *Roma* (1972) and *Fellini's Casanova* (1976). In Sight & Sound's 2002 poll of directors he was ranked second.

Spanish poet, playwright and theater director, a leading member of the Generation of '27 that introduced European movements such as symbolism, futurism and surrealism into Spanish literature. He rose to fame with *Romancero gitano* (*Gypsy Ballads*, 1928), a book of poems depicting life in his native [[Andalusia]] that combined traditional motifs with avant-garde styles. After a stay in [[New York City]] from 1929 to 1930, he wrote the plays *Blood Wedding* (1932), *Yerma* (1934) and *The House of Bernarda Alba* (1936). He was assassinated by Nationalist forces at the start of the [[Spanish Civil War]], and his remains have never been found. The motive remains in dispute.

Conscious subjective experience of [[Emotion|emotion]] or sensation. The term is closely related to, but not the same as, emotion. Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio distinguishes emotions, which are mental images and the bodily changes accompanying them, from feelings, which are the perception of those bodily changes. [[William James]] similarly proposed that feelings result from the perception of bodily changes in response to external stimuli. In the work of [[Carl Jung]], feeling is one of the four primary functions of consciousness, alongside thinking, sensation and intuition. Feeling differs from sensation, which is raw sensory input, and from mood, which is more diffuse and long-lasting. The study of subjective experience is called [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenology]].
